Frames are stuck together with cross comb. This is a mess.

Comb built across multiple frames or at right angles to the frame direction — frames stuck together. Cut the cross comb out carefully during inspection. Realign frames to proper spacing. If the colony persists, use foundation or starter strips to guide comb direction. Cross comb makes inspections impossible and should be corrected early.
 Cross comb usually happens when bees are drawing comb without a guide (no foundation, no starter strip, or frames spaced too wide). Fix early — the longer it goes, the more brood and honey are in the wrong places, and the harder it is to fix without losing bees/brood. Some genetics are more prone to it than others.

We're in the dearth. Spotty brood and most of the capped cells are bullet-shaped drone cells.

This could be several things.
 Differential diagnosis:
  - DroneLayer (85%) — drone-laying queen (lost queen, failed to mate, or queen too old)
  - LayingWorkers (60%) — if no queen cells seen and colony has been queenless >3 weeks

High-confidence diagnosis. Bullet-shaped drone cappings = drones being raised in worker cells. Means only unfertilized eggs are being laid. Distinguish drone-laying queen vs laying workers:
  - Single egg per cell, orderly pattern → drone-laying queen
  - Multiple eggs per cell, eggs on cell walls → laying workers
Drone-laying queen: requeen immediately. Laying workers: combine with another colony — requeening almost always fails.

Season-dependent. In winter/early spring: normal — the colony is clustered tight and only rearing brood where they can keep it warm. In active season with good temperatures: suggests the colony is small or stressed. Check: colony size vs neighbors, food stores, varroa load.

It's October. I'm seeing bees with shriveled, crumpled wings coming out of the cells.

This points to Dwindling. Likely cause: Deformed Wing Virus (DWV) — vectored by varroa. DWV symptoms mean high varroa load has been present for weeks. The virus causes wing deformity and reduced lifespan. ACTION: treat for varroa immediately. If it's during the honey flow, use a treatment that doesn't contaminate honey (formic acid = Mite Away Quick Strips, or thymol after flow). Confirm with an alcohol wash or sugar shake. If >2% mite load: treat. If >5%: colony is in crisis.

There are brown streaks all over the front of the hive and the top bars.

Nosema infection. Dysentery from gut pathogen (Nosema ceranae). Nosema causes dysentery — brown streaks are bee feces. More common in winter/early spring when bees can't fly to defecate. Treat with Fumagillin (Fumidil-B) in syrup, or let the colony clear it naturally once they can take cleansing flights. Check if colony is queenright once they're flying.

What does hairless black bees mean?

Bees that appear hairless, dark/black, shiny — sometimes trembling on frames. This indicates Dwindling (confidence 75%). Hairless black syndrome = CBPV. Often seen in large colonies under varroa pressure. The bees lose body hair, appear shiny and black, and may tremble or be expelled by guard bees. Treat for varroa (reduces the viral load). The colony may recover if mite pressure is brought down quickly.

  - Queenright (25%) — failing queen
  - Queenless (20%) — queen died or failed

Differential diagnosis — do NOT jump to a conclusion. Check: (1) Varroa: alcohol wash or sugar shake. High mite load + spotty brood = virus. (2) Queen: look for eggs. No eggs + spotty = queen failing or gone. (3) Disease: smell (AFB = rotten), rope test, check for chalkbrood mummies. (4) Pesticide: ask about recent spraying in area. (5) Cold snap: if recent dip below 10°C during brood rearing, cold-damaged brood.

It's October. Empty queen cups — just the cup, no egg, no larva. Should I be worried?

That's a clear sign of Queenright. (85% confidence) Queen cups are NOT queen cells. They are play cups — workers draw them on the bottom bars as a normal spring behavior, essentially practicing for swarm season. EMPTY queen cups are harmless. They do not mean the colony is going to swarm. The key distinction: a queen cup becomes a queen cell only when an egg is laid in it and royal jelly is added. Check again at your next inspection — if the cups are still empty, nothing has changed. If there's an egg or larva inside, NOW you have a queen cell and need to assess swarm vs supersedure. Do NOT destroy empty queen cups — the workers will just rebuild them and you'll lose the signal of when they actually start using them.

How often should I rotate my brood comb?

Rotate brood comb every 3-4 years (12-16 brood cycles). Each brood cycle leaves a silk cocoon lining in the cell, darkening the wax and slightly narrowing the cells. After 12+ cycles, bees raised in old comb are smaller, and pesticide/acaricide residues accumulate to concerning levels. Move dark frames to the outside of the brood box so the queen stops laying in them, then remove when empty of brood. Replace with fresh foundation or starter strips.

It's June. The workers have drawn queen cups but there's nothing in them.

That's Queenright — no question. (85% confidence) Queen cups are NOT queen cells. They are play cups — workers draw them on the bottom bars as a normal spring behavior, essentially practicing for swarm season. EMPTY queen cups are harmless. They do not mean the colony is going to swarm. The key distinction: a queen cup becomes a queen cell only when an egg is laid in it and royal jelly is added. Check again at your next inspection — if the cups are still empty, nothing has changed. If there's an egg or larva inside, NOW you have a queen cell and need to assess swarm vs supersedure. Do NOT destroy empty queen cups — the workers will just rebuild them and you'll lose the signal of when they actually start using them.
